title: Sorting & Searching Revision Notes: Big-O, Sorts and Binary Search
summary: Night-before revision of Big-O analysis, the six classic sorts (bubble, insertion, merge, quick, heap, counting) with stability and complexity, and binary search with its common variants.

chapters.title: Big-O and Sorting Mental Model
points: Big-O drops constants and lower-order terms: 3n² + 5n + 2 is O(n²); it is an asymptotic upper bound on growth as n grows, and you state whether it bounds the best, average or worst case
Growth order: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!)
Best, average and worst case differ: quick sort is O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst; always state which case you mean
Space complexity counts extra memory beyond the input: in-place sorts use O(1) or O(log n) stack, merge sort uses O(n)
Stable sort keeps equal keys in original order; in-place sort needs no big auxiliary array; comparison sorts cannot beat Ω(n log n)

chapters.title: Simple Sorts: Bubble and Insertion
points: Bubble sort: repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order pairs; after pass k the k largest are fixed at the end
Bubble optimisation: stop when a full pass makes no swap, giving O(n) best case on sorted input; worst/average O(n²), O(1) space, stable
Insertion sort: grow a sorted prefix by shifting larger elements right and dropping the key into its gap; worst/average O(n²), best O(n) on sorted input, stable, in-place
Insertion sort wins on small or nearly sorted arrays, which is why hybrid sorts (Timsort, introsort) use it for tiny partitions
Bubble does about n²/2 swaps while insertion does shifts only; insertion is almost always the better of the two

chapters.title: Divide and Conquer Sorts: Merge and Quick
points: Merge sort: split in half, sort each recursively, merge two sorted halves with two pointers; always O(n log n), O(n) extra space, stable
Merge stability rule: on ties take from the left half first (use <= when comparing); using < breaks stability
Quick sort: pick a pivot, partition into smaller and larger, recurse; average O(n log n), worst O(n²), in-place with O(log n) stack, not stable

Worst case hits on already sorted input with first/last pivot; fix with random or median-of-three pivot, and recurse on the smaller side while looping on the larger side to bound stack depth at O(log n)
Pick merge for stability, linked lists and guaranteed bounds; pick quick for in-place speed and cache-friendly arrays

chapters.title: Heap Sort and Counting Sort
points: Heap sort: build a max-heap in O(n), then swap root with the last element and sift down, shrinking the heap; O(n log n) always, O(1) space, not stable
Heap indices (0-based): children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2, parent is (i-1)/2; heapify must start from the last non-leaf n/2-1 going down to 0
Counting sort: count occurrences of each key, prefix-sum the counts, then place elements from right to left into the output; O(n + k) time and space
Iterating the output pass right to left is what makes counting sort stable; it only suits integer keys in a small range k, and is the base of radix sort
Non-comparison sorts like counting beat the n log n bound because they index by key value instead of comparing

chapters.title: Binary Search and Its Variants
points: Binary search needs a sorted array; each step halves the range so time is O(log n), space O(1) iterative
Template: lo=0, hi=n-1; while lo<=hi: mid=lo+(hi-lo)/2; compare a[mid] to target, then lo=mid+1 or hi=mid-1; return -1 if not found
Compute mid as lo+(hi-lo)/2, not (lo+hi)/2, which overflows for large indices in fixed-width ints
First/last occurrence: on a match, record the index and keep searching left (hi=mid-1) or right (lo=mid+1)
Search on answer and rotated arrays: binary search any monotonic predicate (min capacity, square root) or decide which half is sorted in a rotated array
Off-by-one traps: mixing lo<=hi with hi=mid (infinite loop) or lo<hi with hi=mid-1 (skips the answer); pick one template and stay consistent

chapters.title: Sorting and Searching Cheat Sheet
points: Time/space table: bubble, insertion O(n²) avg, O(1); merge O(n log n), O(n); quick O(n log n) avg, O(n²) worst, O(log n); heap O(n log n), O(1); counting O(n+k), O(n+k)
Stable: bubble, insertion, merge, counting. Not stable: quick, heap (typical implementations)
Best-case O(n): bubble (with early exit) and insertion on sorted input; merge and heap stay O(n log n) regardless
Choosing: tiny or nearly sorted → insertion; need stable and guaranteed → merge; fastest general in-memory → quick; O(1) space with guarantee → heap; small integer keys → counting
Binary search: O(log n), mid=lo+(hi-lo)/2, lo<=hi loop, lower bound = first index >= target (first occurrence), upper bound = first index > target (last occurrence is upper bound - 1)
